paragraphs: This paper asks which measures of a generative model’s quality can actually be estimated reliably from a finite test dataset. Its starting point is the gap between classification, where error rates have a clear interpretation, and open-ended generation, where choosing a meaningful metric does not automatically make that metric statistically measurable.

The authors develop a theoretical framework for language-model evaluation and distinguish two families of metrics. Test-based metrics compare distributions through a collection of tests. For integral probability metrics built from bounded tests, they establish finite-sample evaluation with both multiplicative and additive approximation errors. A further restriction on the complexity of the test collection, finite fat-shattering dimension, permits arbitrary precision.

The result differs for similarity measures such as Rényi and KL divergences: rare events can determine their values, preventing finite-sample evaluability in the framework studied. The paper also examines perplexity’s possibilities and limits. The contribution is a way to separate a metric’s conceptual appeal from whether observed samples can reliably support its numerical value.
icml-2026-a-theoretical-framework-for-st.tldr: A theoretical framework identifies which generative-model evaluation metrics admit finite-sample guarantees and why rare events obstruct others.

paragraphs: Deep research systems can retrieve information, reason over it, and produce long reports, but a long autonomous run can drift away from what a user currently wants. SteER addresses this problem by making user interaction part of the research process, allowing direction to change after the initial request has been scoped.

At decision points, the framework weighs the costs and benefits of asking for input against continuing independently. Its planning encourages diverse research directions, while utility signals favor alignment with the user, new information, and coverage. A live persona model changes during the session, giving later decisions an updated representation of the user rather than relying entirely on the opening query.

The authors report alignment improvements of up to 22.80% over the evaluated open-source and proprietary baselines, leading results on breadth and balance, and human preference in more than 85% of pairwise alignment judgments. They also introduce a persona–query benchmark and a data-generation pipeline. These findings support selective, interpretable interaction as a useful component of long research workflows.
icml-2026-an-interactive-paradigm-for-de.tldr: SteER decides when research agents should seek user input, improving reported alignment and report quality through mid-process steering.

paragraphs: This paper studies how repeated self-attention updates move token representations, connecting those movements to optimization. It first analyzes the zero-temperature limit, where attention becomes a hard selection rule. In that limit, an update can be interpreted as a Frank-Wolfe step on a quadratic objective over the convex hull of the current tokens.

The resulting behavior depends on the key-query matrix. When it is negative semidefinite, the quadratic energy converges at a sublinear O(t⁻¹) rate. In the positive semidefinite case, extending the rule across the convex hull produces Voronoi cells. Interior points remain in their starting cells and move straight toward the corresponding vertices, with exponential convergence when the step size stays bounded away from zero. The authors also establish well-posedness of the associated continuous-time limit.

For finite inverse temperature β, a Markov-chain analysis establishes dynamic metastability: tokens quickly approach vertices and, with high probability, remain nearby for times exponential in β before eventual collapse. This explains how the hard-selection approximation can remain accurate over exponentially long horizons.
icml-2026-attentions-forward-pass-and-fr.tldr: Self-attention’s hardmax limit connects to Frank-Wolfe optimization and explains long-lived near-vertex behavior at finite temperature.

paragraphs: When several language models answer a question, majority voting provides a simple way to choose a collective answer. Its weakness is that every vote counts equally, even when models differ in reliability or their answers are correlated. Agreement can therefore conceal information about which models contributed it and how their responses relate.

The paper introduces two aggregation algorithms, Optimal Weight and Inverse Surprising Popularity. Both use first-order and second-order information to account for differences and relationships that ordinary voting overlooks. The methods form a training-free aggregation framework, so the contribution concerns how existing model outputs are combined. Under assumptions the authors describe as mild, their analysis proves that the methods mitigate inherent limitations of majority voting.

The evaluation covers synthetic data, UltraFeedback, MMLU, and the ARMMAN healthcare setting. Across these reported experiments, the algorithms consistently outperform standard baselines. The findings support a more informative approach to collective decisions: the pattern behind agreement can matter alongside the number of models choosing an answer.
icml-2026-beyond-majority-voting-llm-agg.tldr: Two training-free aggregation methods use model differences and correlations to improve collective LLM decisions beyond majority voting.

paragraphs: Self-Optimizing Language Models address the mismatch between a uniform computation budget and the varying difficulty of generated tokens. A lightweight policy reads a frozen language model’s hidden state and chooses an efficiency action at each decoding step. Those actions can adjust attention sparsity, structured pruning of MLP activations, and activation quantization precision while preserving the base model’s weights.

The policy learns through group-relative policy optimization on teacher-forced sequences. Each training episode keeps the token sequence fixed and samples different computation schedules for that same sequence. Comparing their likelihoods under identical supervision helps evaluate how the schedules affect quality. The reward balances language-model quality with soft penalties encouraging average computation to match a requested budget.

Across the tested models and computation regimes, the method improves quality at matched budgets relative to static allocation and strong random schedule search. The authors report a better quality–efficiency frontier in all their experiments and MMLU accuracy improvements of up to 7.3% over uniform allocation. These findings support learning where computation is most useful within a single model.
icml-2026-compute-where-it-counts-self-o.tldr: A learned policy allocates computation token by token, improving measured language-model quality at matched budgets without changing base weights.

paragraphs: Robotic control requires both organizing sensory information into a useful account of the current situation and planning actions with future consequences in mind. This paper treats these as intertwined problems. It motivates active inference as a framework for addressing both, drawing on its account of how biological brains combine perception and action.

The authors identify a gap between that broad perspective and its use in artificial intelligence: existing applications have largely extended model-based approaches. Their contribution is a formal abstraction covering model-based, distributional, and model-free reinforcement learning algorithms. This common formulation provides a route for integrating active inference into distributional reinforcement learning.

The key consequence claimed is that active inference’s performance advantages become accessible without modeling transition dynamics. That matters because the proposed connection reaches beyond approaches that explicitly model how actions change the environment. The paper’s central contribution is therefore a unification of algorithmic perspectives, linking sensory organization and far-sighted control through a distributional reinforcement learning formulation.
icml-2026-distributional-active-inferenc.tldr: A formal abstraction integrates active inference into distributional reinforcement learning without requiring a transition-dynamics model.

paragraphs: An action that sounds routine can become unlawful because of its surrounding circumstances. This paper evaluates whether frontier AI models recognize that dependence on context. Its four corporate-law scenarios involve editing documents, trading stock, requesting payment, and approving communications, with circumstances such as investigations or bankruptcy filings changing whether an action is lawful.

The study tests both conversational and agentic settings and includes a human baseline. This design examines more than whether a model refuses an obviously unlawful instruction: successful behavior requires following lawful requests while refusing requests made unlawful by the scenario. Excessive refusal is therefore a distinct failure, because a model can avoid prohibited actions while still mishandling legitimate work.

The best-performing models consistently made the intended lawful–unlawful distinction, although results varied substantially across models and scenarios. Reasoning models and agentic environments showed higher performance in the study. The contribution is a controlled evaluation methodology that can be extended to additional legal scenarios and domains, with context-sensitive compliance as its target.
icml-2026-evaluating-contextual-illegali.tldr: Controlled corporate-law scenarios test whether AI models distinguish lawful requests from routine actions made unlawful by context.

paragraphs: Principal component analysis can require repeated matrix-vector products that are only approximately available, including when computation is decentralized. The Accelerated Noisy Power Method addresses this setting. Earlier guarantees showed faster convergence than the standard noisy method, but required perturbations to be so small that the results had limited practical applicability.

This paper improves the analysis while retaining the accelerated convergence rate. Its main advance is to permit substantially milder conditions on the errors in matrix-vector products. The authors also establish worst-case optimality: within the analyzed setting, neither the convergence rate nor the permitted noise conditions can be improved without losing convergence guarantees.

The analysis leads to an accelerated decentralized PCA algorithm with communication costs similar to those of non-accelerated alternatives. Thus, its theoretical improvement supports faster convergence without requiring a corresponding increase in communication costs. The authors describe it, to their knowledge, as the first decentralized PCA algorithm with provably accelerated convergence, connecting a sharper perturbation analysis to a distributed computational setting.
icml-2026-improved-analysis-of-the-accel.tldr: A sharper noise analysis preserves accelerated PCA convergence under milder perturbations and yields a provably accelerated decentralized algorithm.

paragraphs: This paper studies whether a planning system can learn reusable strategies that work on new combinations and much larger problems. Classical planning offers explicit descriptions of relationships, allowing the authors to focus on this generalization challenge without also learning perception. Sparse rewards make ordinary reinforcement-learning exploration difficult in the settings considered.

The proposed framework combines weighted A-star search with a value heuristic represented by a Relational Graph Neural Network. The heuristic guides which possibilities search explores, and the resulting search data improves the heuristic through Q-learning. This creates a self-improving loop in which search produces learning material and learning makes the search guidance more useful.

The learned heuristics can also act as general policies, solving new instances without search. The authors demonstrate this behavior on Sokoban, PushWorld, The Witness, and planning-competition benchmarks where deep reinforcement learning otherwise fails. A striking example is Blocksworld: training on instances with fewer than 30 blocks yields heuristics that solve instances with 488 blocks without search, demonstrating strong zero-shot generalization in that reported setting.
icml-2026-learning-to-search-and-searchi.tldr: A search-and-Q-learning loop learns relational planning heuristics that can generalize to much larger problems and sometimes solve them without search.

paragraphs: LOGDIFF studies how to guide diffusion models using complex logical requirements at generation time. The question is whether guidance for individual attributes or constraints can be combined into an exact guidance signal for a larger Boolean formula. The framework makes the conditions for that composition explicit.

The authors derive a Boolean calculus with a sufficient condition for exactness. A formula must admit a circuit in which conjunctions join conditionally independent subformulas, while disjunctions join subformulas that are conditionally independent or mutually exclusive. Under those conditions, a recursive algorithm computes exact guidance from atomic scores and posterior probabilities. For commonly encountered classes of distributions, they also show that any Boolean formula can be compiled into a suitable circuit.

A hybrid method combines atomic guidance scores with estimated posterior probabilities, connecting classifier guidance and classifier-free guidance. It applies both to logical composition and ordinary conditional generation. Image and protein-structure experiments demonstrate the framework’s effectiveness, while the theoretical contribution identifies when combining simple constraints supports exact guidance for more elaborate requirements.
icml-2026-logical-guidance-for-the-exact.tldr: LOGDIFF gives sufficient conditions and an efficient calculus for composing exact diffusion guidance from simpler logical constraints.

paragraphs: Med-SegLens examines the internal features of medical image segmentation models to explain why they fail when data changes. It uses sparse autoencoders to decompose activations from SegFormer and U-Net into interpretable latent features. Comparing these features provides a way to study model behavior beneath the final segmentation output.

The framework aligns latents across architectures and datasets spanning healthy, adult, pediatric, and sub-Saharan African glioma cohorts. The authors identify a stable set of shared representations, alongside differences in how strongly models rely on population-specific features. Their analysis links dataset shift to this differential reliance and shows that the implicated latents function as causal bottlenecks for segmentation failures.

Targeted changes to those latents correct errors and improve adaptation across datasets without retraining. In the reported results, interventions recover performance in 70% of failure cases and raise Dice score from 39.4% to 74.2%. The contribution connects interpretation to intervention: comparing internal representations can help locate specific failure mechanisms and provide a direct way to address them.
icml-2026-med-seglens-latent-level-model.tldr: Med-SegLens compares interpretable internal features across segmentation models and datasets, enabling targeted error correction without retraining.

paragraphs: MemoryBench asks whether a language-model system can improve from user feedback accumulated while it is in service. This shifts the evaluation target beyond remembering information from a long input. The authors argue that many existing memory benchmarks concentrate on similar reading-comprehension tasks and therefore do not adequately test learning through continued use.

The paper introduces a framework for simulating user feedback and a benchmark spanning multiple domains, languages, and task types. That breadth makes accumulated feedback central to the evaluation while moving beyond a single task format. The motivation is to assess memory and continual learning as routes to improvement alongside scaling training data, model size, and inference computation.

Experiments find that the evaluated state-of-the-art baselines fall short in both effectiveness and efficiency. The benchmark therefore exposes difficulties in making useful learning from feedback practical within language-model systems. Its contribution is an evaluation setting for studying that ability, giving future memory mechanisms and optimization methods a target grounded in ongoing interaction rather than long-input comprehension alone.
icml-2026-memorybench-a-benchmark-for-me.tldr: MemoryBench evaluates whether LLM systems learn effectively and efficiently from accumulated user feedback across varied tasks, languages, and domains.

paragraphs: Forecasting across locations requires understanding both how individual locations behave and how their behavior changes together over time. This paper targets the difficulty of capturing those interactions under substantial noise. It argues that physical spatial relationships alone do not adequately address evolving temporal correlations and systematic forecasting errors.

The proposed framework organizes prediction into nested spatial scales. It first uses spectral clustering to construct semantically coherent regions, then combines predicted regional trends with historical observations at individual nodes. A progressive coarse-to-fine predictor injects these larger-scale future dynamics into detailed forecasts. The regional information is an abstract future representation produced within the forecasting approach, providing top-down guidance for local predictions.

Experiments on multiple real-world datasets show consistent improvements over the evaluated state-of-the-art baselines. These findings support the usefulness of connecting the broad direction of a region’s future behavior with finer local histories. The contribution is a forecasting structure that explicitly brings those two levels together to model complex spatial and temporal interactions.
icml-2026-nested-spatio-temporal-time-se.tldr: A nested forecasting framework uses predicted regional trends to guide finer-grained forecasts from local historical observations.

paragraphs: PASA addresses a weakness of text watermarking: paraphrasing can change wording while retaining meaning, undermining signals tied to specific vocabulary choices. The method embeds and detects its watermark at the semantic level. Its aim is to keep generated text identifiable through meaning-preserving changes while maintaining text quality.

The algorithm operates on semantic clusters in an embedding space. It creates a statistical dependency between token sequences and auxiliary sequences using shared randomness synchronized through a secret key and semantic history. The authors ground this mechanism in a theoretical framework that characterizes a jointly optimal embedding-and-detection pair and the fundamental trade-offs between detection accuracy, robustness, and distortion.

Across the evaluated language models and meaning-preserving attacks, PASA remains robust even under strong paraphrasing and preserves high text quality. It outperforms the tested vocabulary-space baselines, while ablations support the effectiveness of its hyperparameter choices. The paper presents the method as distortion-free, connecting its semantic construction to a principled treatment of watermarking quality and resilience.
icml-2026-pasa-a-principled-embedding-sp.tldr: PASA places watermarks in semantic embedding space and shows robustness to strong paraphrasing while preserving text quality.

paragraphs: An embodied agent needs a description of its surroundings that includes the details relevant to its next decision. A standalone vision-language model can overlook those details, leaving a gap between seeing a scene and acting effectively within it. PRISM addresses this gap by tightly connecting visual perception with language-model reasoning.

Its dynamic question-and-answer pipeline lets the decision-making language model critique the visual model’s description and ask follow-up questions directed at the current goal. The answers are synthesized into a compact image description. This closed loop makes perception responsive to the task, with reasoning helping determine which visual information needs further attention.

On ALFWorld and Room-to-Room, the authors report significant improvements over state-of-the-art image-based models and systematic, substantial gains from interactive, goal-oriented perception. The pipeline is fully automatic and does not require handcrafted questions or answers. These results support the value of interleaving perception and reasoning during sequential decisions, so the agent’s representation of the scene reflects what it needs to accomplish.
icml-2026-prism-perception-reasoning-int.tldr: PRISM lets a decision-making LLM question a visual model about task-relevant details, improving embodied-agent performance in two benchmarks.

paragraphs: Dynamic graphs represent evolving systems as snapshots taken at different times. A model trained once on historical snapshots can struggle when later snapshots develop new patterns or shift away from the training distribution. PromptDyG addresses this problem in a live-update setting, allowing adaptation as new graph snapshots arrive.

The framework keeps its backbone frozen and learns a dynamic graph prompt during testing. It updates that prompt by minimizing feature-wise entropy without labels, making adaptation possible without supervised feedback on the new snapshots. The prompt provides an adjustable component through which the system can continuously respond to changing graph patterns.

The theoretical analysis shows that this unsupervised prompt adaptation can guarantee a larger similarity margin between positive and negative pairs, supporting more accurate dynamic predictions. Experiments on six benchmark datasets report consistent, significant improvements over state-of-the-art baselines. Together, the analysis and results support prompt adaptation as an efficient way to update predictions for evolving graphs while retaining a fixed underlying model.
icml-2026-promptdyg-test-time-prompt-ada.tldr: PromptDyG adapts prompts without labels as graph snapshots evolve, improving predictions while keeping the backbone frozen.

paragraphs: This paper studies predicting numerical properties of code execution directly from code text. Its Regression Language Model uses a frozen language-model encoder within a unified predictor. The targets span memory use in high-level languages, execution latency of Triton GPU kernels, and the accuracy and speed of neural networks represented in ONNX.

The approach replaces the need for heavy, domain-specific feature engineering with a shared text-based representation. A relatively small 300-million-parameter model based on T5Gemma achieves Spearman rank correlation above 0.9 on APPS programming submissions. A single unified model also exceeds 0.5 average Spearman correlation across 24 programming languages in CodeNet, showing useful ordering of outcomes across varied code settings.

For five classic neural architecture search spaces, the authors report the highest average Kendall-Tau correlation, 0.46, in settings previously dominated by graph neural networks. The model also predicts architecture latency across numerous hardware platforms. These findings support code text as a common basis for predicting several kinds of execution-related numerical outcomes.
icml-2026-regression-language-models-for.tldr: A unified regression model with a frozen language encoder predicts code memory use, kernel latency, and neural-network performance directly from text.

paragraphs: A graph can support both node classification and link prediction, creating opportunities to reuse what a model learns between tasks. This paper argues that such transfer is hard to assess when evaluations use incompatible splits, different observed graphs, or changing negative examples. It introduces a leakage-free protocol with fixed node and edge splits, a shared message-passing graph excluding evaluated edges, and fixed link-prediction negatives.

Across GCN, GraphSAGE, and GPS, transfer depends strongly on direction. Node classification consistently helps link prediction on homophilic graphs. The reverse direction is fragile: simply reusing link-prediction representations can reduce classification accuracy. It becomes reliably helpful mainly when structure dominates, link prediction is easy, and node classification still has room to improve.

These results suggest that link prediction can serve as structural pretraining under suitable conditions. The authors also introduce CoTask Score to summarize joint utility when one encoder serves both tasks. Simple dataset statistics, especially homophily, can help select transfer mechanisms and avoid harmful reuse.
icml-2026-same-graph-cross-task-transfer.tldr: A controlled graph-transfer protocol reveals directional benefits and identifies conditions under which sharing representations helps or harms.

paragraphs: Small language-model agents can handle simple tasks economically, but the authors find that their performance fails to scale with complexity on the deep-search and coding tasks studied. SALE addresses how to allocate work among agents of different sizes, seeking useful contributions from smaller agents while deciding when greater capability is worth its cost.

The framework organizes strategy auctions inspired by freelancer marketplaces. Agents bid by proposing plans, which a cost–value mechanism scores. Shared auction memory helps refine those strategies, supporting per-task routing and continued improvement at test time without training a router. Allocation therefore draws on the plans agents propose for the particular task.

On average, SALE reduces use of the largest agent by 52% and overall cost by 35%, while consistently improving pass@1 with negligible token overhead. The evaluated established routers either underperform the largest agent or do not reduce cost. These results suggest that coordination and strategy refinement can improve the usefulness of smaller agents within a mixed system.
icml-2026-scaling-small-agents-through-s.tldr: SALE routes tasks through auctions of agent plans, reducing average cost and reliance on the largest agent while improving pass@1.

paragraphs: Conformal prediction commonly uses p-values to construct prediction sets, but combining dependent evidence across models or data splits can be restrictive in that formulation. E-values offer additional ways to combine evidence. This paper examines how to move between the two formulations without needlessly enlarging the resulting prediction sets.

The authors show that classical p-to-e conversions do not preserve conformal prediction sets and can make them overly conservative. Their P2E calibrator converts a conformal p-value into an e-value while keeping the original induced prediction set unchanged. Theory and experiments establish that this can produce substantial efficiency gains over existing conversion methods.

The formulation also enables e-value merging and randomization in cross-conformal prediction and conformal aggregation. For both applications, the proposed methods achieve the desired 1−α coverage guarantee while improving efficiency over standard baselines. This strengthens the coverage available from typical cross-conformal variants, which provide only approximate 1−2α coverage. The contribution connects flexible evidence combination with preservation of useful prediction sets.
icml-2026-set-preserving-calibration-fro.tldr: A set-preserving p-to-e calibrator enables efficient conformal evidence combination with 1−α coverage guarantees in two applications.

paragraphs: This paper analyzes stochastic variational inequalities with a focus on min-max optimization over potentially unbounded constraint sets. It removes two assumptions often used in analysis: a bounded domain and a uniform bound on the variance of stochastic estimates. The authors note that bounded variance can fail even for bilinear min-max problems when the domain is unbounded.

The guarantees cover monotone variational inequalities and structured nonmonotone problems that admit a solution to the weak Minty variational inequality. That second condition makes the analysis applicable to a structured class of nonconvex–nonconcave min-max problems. The permitted stochastic oracles can have variance growing as quickly as the squared norm of the optimization variable.

For both problem classes, the authors obtain oracle complexity of Õ(ε⁻⁴) to reduce the expected residual norm below ε. This matches the best-known complexity for constrained variational inequalities, previously obtained in this setting under bounded variance. The advance preserves that rate while accommodating substantially more variable stochastic estimates and unbounded feasible regions.
icml-2026-solving-stochastic-variational.tldr: The analysis matches best-known constrained variational-inequality complexity while allowing unbounded domains and variance that grows quadratically.

paragraphs: TFRBench evaluates the reasoning produced by forecasting systems alongside their numerical predictions. It focuses on whether explanations capture dependencies between channels, temporal trends, and external events. This makes the analysis behind a forecast an explicit evaluation target, addressing a gap in benchmarks centered on numerical accuracy alone.

To create evaluation material, the authors use a multi-agent framework with repeated verification to synthesize reasoning traces grounded in numerical data. The benchmark spans ten datasets across five domains. Their evaluation finds the traces causally effective and useful for evaluation; prompting language models with them also improves forecasting accuracy relative to direct numerical prediction, with a reported example rising from about 40.2% to 56.6%.

The benchmark experiments show that off-the-shelf language models struggle with both reasoning and numerical forecasting, often missing domain-specific dynamics and receiving lower LLM-as-a-Judge scores. Together, these results support evaluating what a forecasting system says about the data as well as what numbers it predicts, while showing that useful reasoning traces can improve forecasts.
icml-2026-tfrbench-a-reasoning-benchmark.tldr: TFRBench tests forecasting reasoning and shows that verified, numerically grounded reasoning traces can improve LLM forecasting accuracy.

paragraphs: This paper investigates why flow-matching critics work well for value estimation in reinforcement learning. The authors find that explicitly representing return distributions does not explain their success and often reduces performance. They instead attribute the benefits to combining a learned velocity field with an integration procedure used both in training and when producing Q-values.

That combination supports test-time recovery: imperfect intermediate estimates can improve as further integration steps dampen their errors. The authors identify this mechanism as absent from monolithic critics. Training through integration also produces more plastic representations, helping the critic represent changing future temporal-difference targets without overwriting features it has already learned.

The paper formalizes these mechanisms and tests them empirically. In high-UTD regimes, the authors report more than twice the performance of monolithic critics and five to ten times higher sample efficiency. The findings point to the interaction between learned dynamics and iterative value readout as a source of the gains, with representational adaptability providing an additional benefit during learning.
icml-2026-what-does-flow-matching-bring-.tldr: The paper attributes flow-matching critics’ gains to iterative error recovery and adaptable representations, with strong reported benefits in high-UTD regimes.

paragraphs: A benchmark loses usefulness when its results no longer clearly distinguish models. This paper studies that saturation problem systematically, treating benchmark longevity as something that can be examined across evaluation designs. The concern matters because benchmarks are used both to track progress and to inform decisions about deploying models.

The authors define saturation and analyze 60 language-model benchmarks using 14 properties related to it. Nearly half of the studied benchmarks exhibit saturation, and saturation rates rise with benchmark age. This establishes that the issue is widespread within the analyzed collection and connects its prevalence to how long a benchmark has been in use.

The study also finds that expert curation affects resilience to saturation, whereas public availability of test data does not show the same influence. These findings suggest that evaluation design choices can help extend a benchmark’s useful life. The contribution is an empirical basis for thinking about durable evaluation: measuring progress requires attention to whether the measuring instrument continues to separate models.
icml-2026-when-ai-benchmarks-plateau-a-s.tldr: A study of 60 language-model benchmarks finds widespread saturation and links resilience to expert curation rather than public test-data availability.

paragraphs: WIND aims to handle many weather and climate tasks with one pretrained model and no task-specific fine-tuning. It learns a general atmospheric prior through self-supervised video reconstruction. An unconditional video diffusion model repeatedly reconstructs atmospheric dynamics from noisy states, learning a representation that can be used across different downstream problems.

At inference time, each task is expressed as an inverse problem and solved through posterior sampling. This lets the same model support probabilistic forecasting, spatial and temporal downscaling, recovery of spatial fields from sparse observations, and enforcement of global dry-air mass conservation. Task requirements enter through the inference problem rather than a separate round of model fine-tuning.

The authors also demonstrate exploration of extreme weather under prescribed thermodynamic perturbations outside the training distribution. Across these applications, the paper presents WIND as a computationally efficient alternative to a landscape of specialized atmospheric models. Its central contribution is the combination of generative video modeling and inverse-problem solving to reuse one atmospheric prior for diverse tasks.
icml-2026-wind-weather-inverse-diffusion.tldr: WIND combines a pretrained atmospheric video diffusion model with inverse-problem solving to handle varied weather and climate tasks without task-specific fine-tuning.
